# Runtime governance for AI agents: Policy checks without changing agent code


[Ayush Jain](https://medium.com/@jain.ayush.94?source=post_page---byline--b75c26feb6c8-----------------------------------------)


14 min read


·


Oct 8, 2026


--


*How the UiPath agentic governance runtime checker checks every agent’s model and tool calls, including agents nobody has touched in months, without any change to agent code.*


***Co-authored with***[Viswanath Lekshmanan](https://medium.com/u/c55401ca263f?source=post_page---user_mention--b75c26feb6c8-----------------------------------------)


S


ay your team built an agent eight months ago. It runs in production, calls a few internal APIs, and nobody has changed the code since. Then a new compliance rule arrives, and someone asks: **does that agent follow it?**


Usually nobody can say without digging into the code. Making the agent follow the rule is a small project of its own: find the owner, update a dependency, test, and redeploy. Now repeat that for every agent you run, including the ones whose owners have moved to other teams.


We wanted to check every agent against the rules without asking anyone to change agent code. That’s why we built the **Runtime Checker** . This post explains what it is, how it gets into every agent, and the design choices that mattered most.


## Who this post is for


Engineers who run AI agents in production and are responsible for what those agents do: **platform teams, SREs, and architects** . We assume you know how LLM agents and tool calls work. You don’t need to have used any governance feature before.


**What you’ll learn:**


- How the checker reaches every agent, including old ones, with no code change.
- The four points in an agent run where it checks: before and after each model call, and before and after each tool call.
- What a rule looks like, with two examples: an agent reading a file it shouldn’t, and an agent promising a customer a refund.
- Why every tenant starts in Audit mode, which records problems without blocking anything, before moving to Enforce mode.
- Why the checker has no dependencies of its own, so it can’t break the agents it runs inside.


## What the Runtime Checker is


The Runtime Checker is a small piece of code that runs inside each agent while the agent works. Whenever the agent is about to call a model or a tool, and whenever it gets a result back, the checker compares what’s happening with your organization’s rules.


A **rule** describes one thing you want to catch, such as “this tool may only read files in the invoice folder.” A set of rules is a **policy** . Admins write rules centrally in UiPath Governance, not in agent code, and the checker downloads the latest rules at the start of every run.


The checker works in one of two modes, set centrally for each tenant (a customer’s workspace in UiPath Automation Cloud™):


- **Audit mode.** The checker records every rule match but blocks nothing. The agent runs exactly as it would without the checker.
- **Enforce mode.** When a rule says to deny a call, the checker stops it.


Every tenant starts in Audit mode. We explain why later in the post.


We built the checker because we needed three things together: checks that reach every agent, checks that see exactly what an agent sends to its tools, and no extra work for agent developers. The next two sections explain how it does that.


## How the checker gets into every agent


To see what an agent sends to its tools, the checker has to run inside the agent’s own process. There are two ways to get it there:


- **An SDK.** Each agent developer adds the checker as a library and calls it from their code.
- **The runtime adds it.** Every UiPath agent job starts inside UiPath Runtime. The runtime can load the checker into the agent’s process before any agent code runs.


An SDK looks simpler, but it has three problems:


- **Coverage depends on each team.** An agent is checked only if its developer added the SDK, and only by the version they installed.
- **Old agents are left out.** An agent built before the SDK existed isn’t checked at all until someone rebuilds and redeploys it.
- **You can’t see the gaps.** An agent without the SDK never reports anything, so it doesn’t appear on any dashboard as a gap. It doesn’t appear at all.


So we chose the second option. When a job starts, the UiPath Runtime loads the checker first. The agent doesn’t import anything, add a dependency, or turn anything on. That gives us three things:


- **Every agent is covered, including old ones.** Coverage follows what actually runs, not what each team installed.
- **One update reaches every agent.** When we improve the checker, every agent picks up the change on its next run, with no rebuild or redeploy.
- **Low-code and coded agents are treated the same.** An agent built in Agent Builder in UiPath Studio and an agent written in Python start in the same runtime, so they get the same checks and report to the same place.

## The four checkpoints


Once the checker is inside the agent, it needs to know when to check. An agent affects the outside world in only two ways: it calls a model, or it calls a tool. So the checker runs at four points in every run. We call these **checkpoints** :


- ` before_model` : before a prompt goes to the model
- ` after_model` : after the model replies, before the reply is used
- ` before_tool` : before a tool runs, with the actual arguments
- ` after_tool` : after the tool returns, with its result


The first` before_model` check also sees the input the agent received, which is where prompt injection usually arrives. So no separate check is needed at the start of the run.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


The four checkpoints on one agent run.


## What a rule looks like


Each rule names a checkpoint, the conditions to test there, and the action to take if the conditions match. The action is one of four:` allow` ,` audit` (record the match),` escalate` (raise it for review), or` deny` (stop the call). The` audit` action is not the same as Audit mode: an action belongs to one rule, while the mode applies to every rule for the tenant.


This simplified rule runs before the` read_file` tool and denies any path outside the invoice folder. In the rule file, the checkpoint goes in the` hook` field:


```text
- name: invoice-tool-stays-in-its-folder    hook: before_tool    severity: high    action: deny            # in Audit mode, recorded as "would have denied"    checks:      - logic: all        conditions:          - field: tool.name            operator: equals            value: read_file          - field: tool.args.path            operator: not_starts_with            value: /data/invoices/
```


Two things to note:


1. **The action and the mode are separate.** The rule says` deny` , but whether the call is actually stopped depends on the tenant's mode. In Audit mode, this deny is only recorded. So you can write the rule you really want on day one and watch what it does before it blocks anything.
2. **The strictest result wins.** If several rules match the same call, deny beats escalate, escalate beats audit, and audit beats allow. The order the rules are written in doesn’t matter.


## Two examples of what it catches


### An agent reads the wrong file


An agent has a file tool and is meant to read invoices from one folder. Then it gets an unclear instruction, or a prompt injection hidden inside a document it’s processing, and it calls the same tool with a different path: a config folder, an HR share, or a folder that holds credentials.


The tool won’t object. The path is valid and the agent has permission. At` before_tool` , the checker sees the exact path before anything is opened. The rule above matches, and in Enforce mode the read never happens. A log would only tell you afterwards that the file tool was used.


Most risky tool use looks like this. It’s rarely an agent using a tool it was never given. It’s an agent using a tool it does have, with arguments nobody expected.


### An agent makes a promise you didn’t approve


A customer-facing agent gets a question its instructions don’t cover, and tries to be helpful:


> “We’ll refund that for you in full.” ** “I can guarantee delivery by Friday.” ** “Yes, that’s covered under your plan.”


Nobody wrote those sentences, and they aren’t in any document the agent was given. The model produced them because agreeing seemed like the right answer.


On paper, the run looks fine: no errors, no tool misuse, and a happy customer. But your company now has a promise to keep that it never made.


At` after_model` , the checker sees the reply before it's sent. This check works differently from the file example. It doesn't compare a path. It reads the text and looks for language that sounds like a promise, a guarantee, or a commitment.

## Why every tenant starts in Audit mode


Most conditions in a rule are simple comparisons, like *equals* , *starts with* , or *is in this list* . They behave exactly as you’d expect. A few checks are fuzzier: spotting a promise in text, unusual characters, or content that looks scrambled to hide what it is. These are some of the most useful checks, but you can’t know how often they’ll flag normal traffic until you run them on your real traffic.


If you find that out when a production job gets blocked in the middle of the night, teams will start looking for ways to switch the checker off. So in Audit mode:


- Every rule is checked, and every match is recorded.
- Nothing is blocked. A deny or escalate is recorded as “would have denied,” and the run continues.
- Agents behave exactly as before: same speed, same outputs, same success rate.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


The same run and the same rule, in Audit mode and in Enforce mode.


What you gain is visibility: which rules would have fired, on which agents, at which checkpoint, and how often. The results show up in two places:


- **Per-run traces** in UiPath Automation Cloud, next to everything else the agent did, so you can see why a run was flagged or stopped.
- **A fleet view** across all your agents: which rules match most, on which agents, and how that changes over time. This is where you decide which rules are safe to enforce.


Both use the same trace ID, so you can go from a spike in the fleet view to the exact run behind it. Recording results never slows the agent down: results are sent in the background, and if a logging endpoint is slow, the checker stops waiting on it.


After a few weeks, the talk about enforcement changes. Instead of “let’s turn it on and hope,” it becomes “this rule matches all the time, and nearly every match is one internal tool doing something normal, so let’s fix the rule first.” You tune rules with evidence, and you know what enforcing will cost before you switch it on.


Switching a tenant from Audit to Enforce is a server-side setting. It arrives with the rules on the next run, so no agent has to change. If a rule turns out to be too strict, it’s fixed the same way.


## What the checker doesn’t check


Because the checker sits inside every agent, it’s tempting to put every check there. We don’t. Agent traffic is already checked in other places, and some checks work better there:


- **Checks that need an AI model to decide** , such as content safety, personal data (personally identifiable information, or PII), and prompt injection detection, run as **guardrails** : a shared central service where each detector is set up once and used by every product.
- **Simple text checks on prompts and model replies** can run in **UiPath AI Trust Layer** , which model calls from UiPath products already pass through.


The checker handles what those places can’t see:


- **Tool calls.** Tool arguments and tool results never pass through AI Trust Layer.
- **What the agent is allowed to do** , such as which tools and folders its builder said it may use.
- **Checks that span several steps of a run.** For example: “flag the run if the agent calls` send_email` more than 20 times," or "flag the run if the agent reads a customer record and then emails an outside address." To apply these, the checker has to remember earlier steps, and only something inside the agent sees the whole run.


Speed matters too. A check inside the agent takes microseconds. Calling a remote service at every tool step would add a network call dozens of times per run. And when a check needs to block, blocking inside the agent is immediate.


When the same detection logic is needed in more than one place, we share it as a library instead of writing it twice.


There’s one more boundary: **if a product already has a setting for something and the customer has set it, that setting decides, not the checker.** For example, say an admin has already set up PII protection for model calls in AI Trust Layer. The checker then doesn’t run its own PII check on those same model calls. If it did, two places would be deciding the same thing, every match would be counted twice on dashboards, and the checker might block something the admin chose to allow.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Where each kind of check runs, and what each place can see.


## What happens when the checker can’t run


The checker needs the UiPath Governance service to get its rules, so we had to decide what happens when that fails. We made two choices:


- **If the checker can’t start, the agent runs anyway.** Governance service unreachable, no rules returned, or rules that don’t load: in each case the agent runs without checks. A problem on our side should not become an outage on yours.
- **If a rule in Enforce mode says no, the answer is no.** The call is stopped.


The first choice has a cost. From the outside, a run without checks looks the same as a run that passed them. So an unchecked run has to be as visible on dashboards as a rule violation, and a run marked as checked has to be able to prove the checker actually ran. We need those signals before enforcing widely. We don’t need them to audit, which is one more reason every tenant starts in Audit mode.


## Staying out of the agent’s way


The runtime loads the checker into the agent’s own Python process. That process already has its own libraries, which the agent’s developer chose and pinned to specific versions. For example, a coded agent might use a particular version of` pydantic` to validate data and of` httpx` to make HTTP calls. The checker now shares that process, so anything it brings with it can clash with what the agent already uses. And if the checker breaks even one agent, the owner will ask for it to be turned off everywhere.


So we built the checker around four rules. Each one prevents a specific way it could break an agent.


**1. The checker brings no libraries of its own.**


- **The risk:** say the checker needed version 2 of` pydantic` and the agent uses version 1. Python can load only one version of a library in a process. Whichever version loses, either the agent or the checker breaks, often with an error that points nowhere near the real cause.
- **What we did:** the checker uses only Python’s standard library, which every agent already has. Where we needed a little extra code, we copied it into the checker under a private name that no agent would ever import, so it can’t clash with anything.


**2. When both use the same library, the agent’s version wins.**


- **The risk:** Python finds libraries by searching a list of folders in order and using the first match. This list is called the import path. If the checker’s folder came first and held a library the agent also uses, Python would quietly load the checker’s copy instead of the agent’s. The agent would behave differently without anyone changing its code.
- **What we did:** the checker’s folder is added to the end of the import path. Python always finds the agent’s libraries first.


**3. Optional features switch off instead of failing.**


- **The risk:** a few checker features only work when a certain library is already installed in the agent’s environment. If the checker required that library, every agent without it would fail when it started.
- **What we did:** the checker loads those libraries only when a feature first needs them. If a library isn’t there, that one feature is skipped and everything else keeps working.


**4. Everything is plain Python.**


- **The risk:** some Python packages include compiled code, written in languages like C or Rust, to run faster. Compiled code must be built separately for every combination of Python version, operating system, and CPU type, for example Python 3.11 on Linux with an Intel CPU, or Python 3.12 on Linux with an ARM CPU. Miss one combination and the checker can’t load on agents that use it. Because the agent runs anyway when the checker can’t start, those agents would run with no checks at all, and nobody would notice.
- **What we did:** the checker and all the code it carries are plain Python, which runs the same on every combination. There is no build to miss.


These rules also keep the checker small and fast: a few hundred kilobytes in size, loaded once when the job starts, and under a millisecond per check. That matters for the same reason as everything else in this section. If teams could feel the checker slowing their agents down, they would push to turn it off.


## Open challenges


Putting the checker in the runtime answers the coverage question. Some hard questions are still open. They aren’t specific to UiPath: anyone who checks agents at run time will meet them.


**Proving that a check really happened.** Because the agent runs anyway when the checker can’t start, a run without checks looks the same as a run that passed them. Flagging a run that sent no results is the easy half. The harder half is proving that a run marked as checked had every call go through the checker. That proof is what an auditor will ask for.


**Making fuzzy checks accurate.** A check that looks for promises in a reply will sometimes flag a normal reply and sometimes miss a real promise. Audit mode lets you see those mistakes before they cost anything. But each customer’s traffic is different, and checks that need less tuning for each one are still an open problem.


**Agents that call other agents.** The checker sees everything inside one agent’s run. More and more work is now split across several agents, where one agent hands a task to the next. A rule like “customer data must not leave the company” may need to follow that data across the whole chain. That means checks in different agents have to share what they have seen.


**Turning written policy into rules.** Compliance standards are written in plain language, such as “access to personal data must be controlled.” Someone has to turn a sentence like that into concrete rules: which tools, which fields, and which checkpoints. Doing this well, and keeping the rules in step as the standard changes, is still hard work.


## Key takeaways


- **Let the runtime add the checker.** Coverage then follows what actually runs, not what each team installed, and old agents are covered too.
- **Check at four checkpoints.** Checkpoints occur before and after each model call, and before and after each tool call. That’s where an agent touches the outside world.
- **Keep rules as data.** Write them centrally and fetch them on each run, so rules and the Audit/Enforce setting can change without touching agents.
- **Start in Audit mode.** Record everything, block nothing, and tune rules on real traffic before enforcing.
- **Don’t check everything in the agent.** Leave model-based checks to guardrails and model traffic checks to AI Trust Layer, and respect settings the customer has already configured.
- **Let agents run if the checker can’t start, but stop calls when a rule says no.** And make unchecked runs easy to see.
- **Don’t break the agent you run inside.** No libraries of its own, plain Python only, and the agent’s libraries always win.


## Closing thought


Governance usually means work for agent teams: a new dependency, a new version, more testing, another release. That’s why it often stalls halfway through the rollout. Moving the checker into the runtime removes most of that work. Existing agents are covered without changes, you can see what your rules would do before they block anything, and when you do switch on Enforce mode, you decide with real data instead of a guess.
